In [[number theory]], '''Fermat's Last Theorem''' (sometimes called '''Fermat's conjecture''', especially in older texts) states that there are no [[Natural number|positive integers]] <math>a, b, c, n</math> with <math>n > 2</math> such that <math>a^n + b^n = c^n</math>.{{sfn|Wiles|1995|loc=Abstract|p=443}} The cases <math>n=1</math> and <math>n=2</math> have been known since antiquity to have infinitely many solutions.{{sfn|Singh|2022|pp=18–20}}

The proposition was first stated as a theorem by [[Pierre de Fermat]] around 1637 in the margin of a copy of ''[[Arithmetica]]''. Fermat added that he had a proof that was too large to fit in the margin. Although other statements claimed by Fermat without proof were subsequently proven by others and credited as theorems of Fermat (for example, [[Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares]]), Fermat's Last Theorem resisted proof, leading to doubt that Fermat ever had a correct proof. Consequently, the proposition became known as a [[conjecture]] rather than a theorem. After 358 years of effort by mathematicians, [[Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem|the first successful proof]] was released in 1994 by [[Andrew Wiles]] and formally published in 1995. It was described as a "stunning advance" in the citation for Wiles's [[Abel Prize]] award in 2016.<ref name="abelcitation">{{Cite web |url=http://www.abelprize.no/c67107/binfil/download.php?tid=67059 |title=Abel Prize 2016 |access-date=16 March 2016 |archive-date=20 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200520195920/https://www.abelprize.no/c67107/binfil/download.php?tid=67059 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It also proved much of the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture, subsequently known as the [[modularity theorem]], and opened up entire new approaches to numerous other problems and mathematically powerful [[lift (mathematics)|modularity lifting]] techniques.

The unsolved problem stimulated the development of [[algebraic number theory]] in the 19th and 20th centuries. For its influence within mathematics and in culture more broadly, it is among the most notable theorems in the [[history of mathematics]].

{{TOC limit|3}}

== Overview ==
=== Pythagorean origins ===
The [[Pythagorean theorem|Pythagorean equation]], <math>x^2+y^2=z^2</math>, has an infinite number of positive [[integer]] solutions for <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>, and <math>z</math>; these solutions are known as [[Pythagorean triple]]s (with the simplest example being 3, 4, 5). Around 1637, Fermat wrote in the margin of a book that the more general equation <math>a^n+b^n=c^n</math> had no solutions in positive integers if <math>n</math> is an integer greater than 2. Although he claimed to have a general [[mathematical proof|proof]] of his conjecture, Fermat left no details of his proof, and none has ever been found. His claim was discovered some 30&nbsp;years later, after his death. This claim, which came to be known as ''Fermat's Last Theorem'', stood unsolved for the next three and a half centuries and was solved with mathematics Fermat would not have known.<ref name="BostonFLTproof">{{Cite web |url=https://www.math.wisc.edu/~boston/869.pdf |first=Nigel|last= Boston|author-link=Nigel Boston |page=5 |title=The Proof of Fermat's Last Theorem |access-date=6 April 2019 |archive-date=23 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190923003312/https://www.math.wisc.edu/~boston/869.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The claim eventually became one of the most notable unsolved problems of mathematics. Attempts to prove it prompted substantial development in [[number theory]], and over time Fermat's Last Theorem gained prominence as an [[List of unsolved problems in mathematics|unsolved problem in mathematics]].

=== Subsequent developments and solution ===
The special case <math>n=4</math>, proved by Fermat himself, is sufficient to establish that if the theorem is false for some [[exponent]] <math>n</math> that is not a [[prime number]], it must also be false for some smaller <math>n</math>, so only prime values of <math>n</math> need further investigation.<ref group=note>If the exponent <math>n</math> were not prime or 4, then it would be possible to write <math>n</math> either as a product of two smaller integers (<math>n=pq</math>), in which <math>p</math> is a prime number greater than 2, and then <math>a^n=a^{pq}=(a^q)^p</math> for each of <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math>. That is, an equivalent solution would ''also'' have to exist for the prime power <math>p</math> that is ''smaller'' than <math>n</math>; or else as <math>n</math> would be a power of 2 greater than 4, and writing <math>n=4q</math>, the same argument would hold.</ref> Over the next two centuries (1637–1839), the conjecture was proved for only the primes 3, 5, and 7, although [[Sophie Germain]] innovated and proved an approach that was relevant to an entire class of primes.{{sfn|Edwards|1996|pages=39–75, 80–86}}{{sfn|Ribenboim|1979|pp=54–56}} In the mid-19th century, [[Ernst Kummer]] extended this and proved the theorem for all [[regular prime]]s, leaving irregular primes to be analyzed individually.{{sfn|Edwards|1996|pages=39–75, 80–86}}{{sfn|Stewart|Tall|2002|pages=183–198}} Building on Kummer's work and using sophisticated computer studies, other mathematicians were able to extend the proof to cover all prime exponents up to four million,<ref name=":0"/> but a proof for all exponents was considered exceedingly difficult or unachievable with the knowledge of the time.{{sfn|Singh|2022|p=223}}

Around 1955, Japanese mathematicians [[Goro Shimura]] and [[Yutaka Taniyama]] suspected a link might exist between [[elliptic curve]]s and [[modular form]]s, two completely different areas of mathematics. Known at the time as the [[Taniyama–Shimura conjecture]], it had no apparent connection to Fermat's Last Theorem. It was widely seen as significant and important in its own right, but was (like Fermat's theorem) considered completely inaccessible to proof.{{sfn|Singh|2022|pp=203–205, 223, 226}}

In 1984, [[Gerhard Frey (mathematician)|Gerhard Frey]] noticed an apparent link between these two previously unrelated and unsolved problems, and he gave an outline suggesting this could be proved.<ref name="Frey1986">{{Cite journal |last=Frey |first=Gerhard|author-link=Gerhard Frey (mathematician) |title=Links between stable elliptic curves and certain Diophantine equations |journal=Annales Universitatis Saraviensis. Series Mathematicae |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=1–40 |year=1986}}</ref>{{sfn|Singh|2022|pp=194-198}} The full proof that the two problems were closely linked was accomplished in 1986 by [[Ken Ribet]], building on a partial proof by [[Jean-Pierre Serre]], who proved all but one part known as the "epsilon conjecture" (see: ''[[Ribet's Theorem]]'' and ''[[Frey curve]]'').<ref name="abelcitation"/> These papers by Frey, Serre and Ribet showed that if the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture could be proven for at least the semi-stable class of elliptic curves, a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem would also follow automatically. The connection is described [[#Equivalent statements of the theorem|below]]: any solution that could contradict Fermat's Last Theorem could also be used to contradict the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture. So if the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture were found to be true, then no solution contradicting Fermat's Last Theorem could exist, meaning that Fermat's Last Theorem must also be true.

Although both problems were daunting and widely considered to be "completely inaccessible" to proof at the time,<ref name="abelcitation"/> this was the first suggestion of a route by which Fermat's Last Theorem could be extended and proved for all numbers, not just some numbers. Unlike Fermat's Last Theorem, the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture was a major active research area and viewed as more within reach of contemporary mathematics.<ref>{{harvnb|Singh|2022|p=144}} quotes Wiles's reaction to this news: ''"I was electrified. I knew that moment that the course of my life was changing because this meant that to prove Fermat's Last Theorem all I had to do was to prove the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture. It meant that my childhood dream was now a respectable thing to work on."''</ref> However, general opinion was that this simply showed the impracticality of proving the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture.{{sfn|Singh|2022|p=144}} Mathematician [[John H. Coates|John Coates]]' quoted reaction was a common one:{{sfn|Singh|2022|p=144}}

{{blockquote|I myself was very sceptical that the beautiful link between Fermat's Last Theorem and the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture would actually lead to anything, because I must confess I did not think that the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture was accessible to proof. Beautiful though this problem was, it seemed impossible to actually prove. I must confess I thought I probably wouldn't see it proved in my lifetime.}}

On hearing that Ribet had proven Frey's link to be correct, English mathematician [[Andrew Wiles]], who had a childhood fascination with Fermat's Last Theorem and had a background of working with elliptic curves and related fields, decided to try to prove the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture as a way to prove Fermat's Last Theorem.{{sfn|Singh|2022|pp=205-226}} In 1993, after six years of working secretly on the problem, Wiles [[Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem|succeeded in proving]] enough of the conjecture to prove Fermat's Last Theorem.{{sfn|Wiles|1995}}{{sfn|Singh|2022|pp=250–277}} Wiles's paper was massive in size and scope. A flaw was discovered in one part of his original paper during [[peer review]] and required a further year and collaboration with a past student, [[Richard Taylor (mathematician)|Richard Taylor]], to resolve.{{sfn|Wiles|1995}}<ref name="Taylor-Wiles1995">{{Cite journal |last1=Taylor |first1=Richard|author1-link=Richard Taylor (mathematician) |last2=Wiles |first2=Andrew|author2-link=Andrew Wiles |title=Ring-theoretic properties of certain Hecke algebras |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |volume=141 |issue=3 |pages=553–572 |year=1995 |doi=10.2307/2118560 |jstor=2118560 === Equivalent statements of the theorem ===
There are several alternative ways to state Fermat's Last Theorem that are mathematically equivalent to the original statement of the problem.

In order to state them, we use the following notations: let <math>\N</math> be the set of natural numbers <math>1,2,3,\dots,</math> let <math>\Z</math> be the set of integers <math>0,\pm 1,\pm 2,\dots,</math> and let <math>\Q</math> be the set of rational numbers <math>a/b</math>, where <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are in <math>\Z</math> with <math>b \neq 0</math>. In what follows we will call a solution to <math>x^n+y^n=z^n</math> where one or more of <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>, or <math>z</math> is zero a ''trivial solution''. A solution where all three are nonzero will be called a ''non-trivial'' solution.

For comparison's sake we start with the original formulation.
* '''Original statement'''. With <math>n,x,y,z\in\N</math> (meaning that <math>n,x,y,z</math> are all positive whole numbers) and <math>n>2</math>, the equation <math>x^n+y^n=z^n</math> has no solutions.

Most popular treatments of the subject state it this way,{{sfn|Edwards|1996|p=3}} though it is sometimes stated over <math>\Z</math>:<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Cox | first = David A. | author-link = David A. Cox
 | doi = 10.1080/00029890.1994.11996897
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[The American Mathematical Monthly]]
 | jstor = 2325116
 | mr = 1252700
 | pages = 3–14
 | title = Introduction to Fermat's last theorem
 | volume = 101
 | year = 1994}}</ref>
* '''Equivalent statement 1:''' {{math|''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, where  <math>n\geq 3</math>, has no non-trivial solutions <math>x, y, z \in \Z</math>.

The equivalence is clear if {{mvar|n}} is even. If {{mvar|n}} is odd and all three of {{math|''x'', ''y'', ''z''}} are negative, then we can replace {{math|''x'', ''y'', ''z''}} with {{math|−''x'', −''y'', −''z''}} to obtain a solution in {{math|'''N'''}}. If two of them are negative, it must be {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|z}} or {{mvar|y}} and {{mvar|z}}. If {{math|''x'', ''z''}} are negative and {{mvar|y}} is positive, then we can rearrange to get {{math|(−''z'')<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} (−''x'')<sup>''n''</sup>}} resulting in a solution in {{math|'''N'''}}; the other case is dealt with analogously. Now if just one is negative, it must be {{mvar|x}} or {{mvar|y}}. If {{mvar|x}} is negative, and {{mvar|y}} and {{mvar|z}} are positive, then it can be rearranged to get {{math|(−''x'')<sup>''n''</sup> + ''z''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''y''<sup>''n''</sup>}} again resulting in a solution in {{math|'''N'''}}; if {{mvar|y}} is negative, the result follows symmetrically. Thus in all cases a nontrivial solution in {{math|'''Z'''}} would also mean a solution exists in {{math|'''N'''}}, the original formulation of the problem.
* '''Equivalent statement 2:''' {{math|''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, where integer {{math|''n'' ≥ 3}}, has no non-trivial solutions {{math|''x'', ''y'', ''z'' ∈ '''Q'''}}.

This is because the exponents of {{math|''x'', ''y'',}} and {{mvar|z}} are equal (to {{mvar|n}}), so if there is a solution in {{math|'''Q'''}}, then it can be multiplied through by an appropriate common denominator to get a solution in {{math|'''Z'''}}, and hence in {{math|'''N'''}}.{{sfn|Edwards|1996|p=3}}
* '''Equivalent statement 3:''' {{math|''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} 1}}, where integer {{math|''n'' ≥ 3}}, has no non-trivial solutions {{math|''x'', ''y'' ∈ '''Q'''}}.

A non-trivial solution {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, {{mvar|c}} ∈ {{math|'''Z'''}} to {{math|''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}} yields the non-trivial solution {{math|''a''/''c''}}, {{math|''b''/''c''}} ∈ {{math|'''Q'''}} for {{math|''v''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''w''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} 1}}. Conversely, a solution {{math|''a''/''b''}}, {{math|''c''/''d''}} ∈ {{math|'''Q'''}} to {{math|''v''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''w''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} 1}} yields the non-trivial solution {{math|''ad'', ''cb'', ''bd''}} for {{math|''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}}.

This last formulation is particularly fruitful, because it reduces the problem from a problem about surfaces in three dimensions to a problem about curves in two dimensions. Furthermore, it allows working over the field {{math|'''Q'''}}, rather than over the ring {{math|'''Z'''}}; [[Field (mathematics)|fields]] exhibit more structure than [[Ring (mathematics)|rings]], which allows for deeper analysis of their elements.

* '''Equivalent statement 4 – reduction to prime exponents:''' If {{tmath|1=n=4}} or {{tmath|n}} is an odd prime number, then {{math|''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}} has no non-trivial solutions <math>x, y, z \in \Z.</math>
The case {{tmath|1=n=4}} was proved already by Fermat and could thus be omitted.

Every positive integer greater than 2 may be written as {{tmath|1=pq}} where either {{tmath|1=p=4}} or {{tmath|p}} is an odd prime number (possibly, {{tmath|1=q=1}}). The equivalence results from the equality <math display=block>x^{pq}+y^{pq}-z^{pq} = (x^q)^p + (y^q)^p-(z^q)^p.</math>
So,every solution for the exponent {{mvar|n}}, if any, provides a solution for the exponent {{mvar|p}}.

* '''Equivalent statement 5 – connection to elliptic curves:''' If {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, {{mvar|c}} is a non-trivial solution to {{math|''a''<sup>''p''</sup> + ''b''<sup>''p''</sup> {{=}} ''c''<sup>''p''</sup>}}, {{mvar|p}} odd prime, then {{math|''y''<sup>''2''</sup> {{=}} ''x''(''x'' − ''a''<sup>''p''</sup>)(''x'' + ''b''<sup>''p''</sup>)}} ([[Frey curve]]) will be an [[elliptic curve]] without a modular form.{{refn|{{harvtxt|Wiles|1995}}: "Frey's suggestion, in the notation of the following theorem, was to show that the (hypothetical) elliptic curve {{math|''y''<sup>''2''</sup> {{=}} ''x''(''x'' + ''u''<sup>''p''</sup>)(''x'' – ''v''<sup>''p''</sup>)}} could not be modular."}}

Examining this elliptic curve with [[Ribet's theorem]] shows that it does not have a [[modular form]]. However, the proof by Andrew Wiles proves that any equation of the form {{math|''y''<sup>''2''</sup> {{=}} ''x''(''x'' − ''a''<sup>''n''</sup>)(''x'' + ''b''<sup>''n''</sup>)}} does have a modular form. Any non-trivial solution to {{math|{{itco|''x''}}<sup>''p''</sup> + {{itco|''y''}}<sup>''p''</sup> {{=}} {{itco|''z''}}<sup>''p''</sup>}} (with {{mvar|p}} an odd prime) would therefore create a [[proof by contradiction|contradiction]], which in turn proves that no non-trivial solutions exist.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Ribet |first=Ken |authorlink=Ken Ribet |title=On modular representations of Gal({{overline|'''Q'''}}/'''Q''') arising from modular forms |journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]] |volume=100 |year=1990 |issue=2 |page=432 |doi=10.1007/BF01231195 |mr=1047143 |url=http://math.berkeley.edu/~ribet/Articles/invent_100.pdf |bibcode=1990InMat.100..431R|hdl=10338.dmlcz/147454 |s2cid=120614740 }}</ref>

In other words, any solution that could contradict Fermat's Last Theorem could also be used to contradict the modularity theorem. So if the modularity theorem were found to be true, then it would follow that no contradiction to Fermat's Last Theorem could exist either. As described above, the discovery of this equivalent statement was crucial to the eventual solution of Fermat's Last Theorem, as it provided a means by which it could be "attacked" for all numbers at once.

== Mathematical history ==
=== Pythagoras and Diophantus ===
==== Pythagorean triples ====
{{Main|Pythagorean triple}}

In ancient times it was known that a triangle whose sides were in the ratio {{math|3:4:5}} would have a right angle as one of its angles. This was used in construction and later in early geometry. It was also known to be one example of a general rule that any triangle where the length of two sides, each squared and then added together {{math|1=(3<sup>2</sup> + 4<sup>2</sup> = 9 + 16 = 25)}}, equals the square of the length of the third side {{math|1=(5<sup>2</sup> = 25)}}, would also be a right angle triangle. This is now known as the [[Pythagorean theorem]], and a triple of numbers that meets this condition is called a Pythagorean triple; both are named after the ancient Greek [[Pythagoras]]. Thus, a Pythagorean triple is a set of three integers {{math|(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} that satisfy the equation{{sfn|Stark|1978|pp=151–155|ps=}} {{math|1=''a''<sup>2</sup> + ''b''<sup>2</sup> = ''c''<sup>2</sup>}}. Examples include {{math|(3, 4, 5)}} and {{math|(5, 12, 13)}}. There are infinitely many such triples,<ref name="Stillwell_2003">{{cite book | last = Stillwell |first=J. | year = 2003 | title = Elements of Number Theory | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=LiAlZO2ntKAC&pg=PA110 | publisher = Springer-Verlag | location = New York | isbn = 0-387-95587-9 | pages = 110–112 | access-date = 2016-03-17| authorlink=John Stillwell }}</ref> and methods for generating such triples have been studied in many cultures, beginning with the [[Babylonian mathematics|Babylonians]]{{sfn|Aczel|1996|pp=13–15|ps=}} and later [[Greek mathematics|ancient Greek]], [[Chinese mathematics|Chinese]], and [[Indian mathematics|Indian]] mathematicians.{{sfn|Singh|2022|pp=18–20}}

==== Diophantine equations ====
{{Main|Diophantine equation}}

Fermat's equation, {{math|1=''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> = ''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}} with positive [[integer]] solutions, is an example of a [[Diophantine equation]],{{sfn|Stark|1978|pp=145–146|ps=}} named for the 3rd-century [[Alexandria]]n mathematician, [[Diophantus]], who studied them and developed methods for the solution of some kinds of Diophantine equations. A typical Diophantine problem is to find two integers {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}} such that their sum, and the sum of their squares, equal two given numbers {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, respectively:
<math display=block>A = x + y, \qquad B= x^2 + y^2.</math>

Diophantus's major work is the ''[[Arithmetica]]'', of which only a portion has survived.{{sfn|Singh|2022|pp= 50–51}} Fermat's conjecture of his Last Theorem was inspired while reading a new edition of the ''Arithmetica'',{{sfn|Stark|1978|p=145|ps=}} that was translated into Latin and published in 1621 by [[Claude Gaspard Bachet de Méziriac|Claude Bachet]].{{sfn|Aczel|1996|pp=44–45|ps=}}{{sfn|Singh|2022|pp=56–58}}

Diophantine equations have been studied for thousands of years. For example, the solutions to the quadratic Diophantine equation {{math|1=''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup> = ''z''<sup>2</sup>}} are given by the [[Pythagorean triple]]s, originally solved by the Babylonians ({{circa|1800 BC}}).{{sfn|Aczel|1996|pp=14–15|ps=}} Solutions to linear Diophantine equations, such as {{math|1=26''x'' + 65''y'' = 13}}, may be found using the [[Euclidean algorithm]] (c. 5th century BC).{{sfn|Stark|1978|pp=44–47|ps=}}
Many [[Diophantine equation]]s have a form similar to the equation of Fermat's Last Theorem from the point of view of algebra, in that they have no ''cross terms'' mixing two letters, without sharing its particular properties. For example, it is known that there are infinitely many positive integers {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}}, and {{mvar|z}} such that {{math|1=''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> = ''z''<sup>''m''</sup>}}, where {{mvar|n}} and {{mvar|m}} are [[relatively prime]] natural numbers.<ref group="note">For example, <math>((k^r+1)^s)^r+(k(k^r+1)^s)^r=(k^r+1)^{rs+1}</math>.</ref>

=== Islamic mathematics ===
The [[cubic equation|cubic]] Fermat equation {{math|1=''x''<sup>3</sup> + ''y''<sup>3</sup> = ''z''<sup>3</sup>}} was studied by [[Abu-Mahmud Khujandi]] ({{circa}} 940–1000), in the period of [[mathematics in the medieval Islamic world]]. He claimed to have proven it to have no integer or rational number solutions, but his proof is now considered faulty.{{sfn|Dickson|1919|p=[https://archive.org/details/historyoftheoryo02dickuoft/page/544/mode/2up 545]|ps=}}<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Al-Khujandi|title=Abu Mahmud Hamid ibn al-Khidr Al-Khujandi|mode=cs1}}</ref><ref>{{cite book
 | last1 = Krantz | first1 = Steven G. | author1-link = Steven G. Krantz
 | last2 = Parks | first2 = Harold R. | author2-link = Harold R. Parks
 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4614-8939-9
 | isbn = 9781461489399
 | page = 316
 | publisher = Springer US
 | title = A Mathematical Odyssey: Journey from the Real to the Complex
 | year = 2014}}</ref> Another mathematician from later in the medieval Islamic period, {{ill|Abdallah ibn Muhhammad ibn Abd al-Razzāq Ibn al-Khawwām|ar|ابن الخوام}} (1243 – after 1324), a student of [[Nasir al-Din al-Tusi]], published a list of open problems among which he included both the degree 3 and degree 4 cases of Fermat's last theorem.<ref>{{cite book|contribution=Vers une étude des aspects historiques et mathématiques des problèmes ouverts d’Ibn al-Khawwām|language=French|contribution-url=https://www.academia.edu/11983583/Vers_une_%C3%A9tude_des_aspects_historiques_et_math%C3%A9matiques_des_probl%C3%A8mes_ouverts_dIbn_al_Khaww%C3%A2m_m_1325_|last1=Abdeljaouad|first1=Mahdi|last2=Hedfi|first2=Hmida|title=Histoire des Mathématiques Arabes|year=1986|pages=157–178}}</ref>

=== Fermat's conjecture ===
[[File:Diophantus-II-8.jpg|thumb|Problem II.8 in the 1621 edition of the {{lang|la|Arithmetica}} of [[Diophantus]]. On the right is the margin that was too small to contain Fermat's alleged proof of his "last theorem".]]
A modern algebraic reformulation of
Problem II.8 of the {{lang|la|[[Arithmetica]]}} asks how a given [[Square (algebra)|squared]] [[rational number]] is split into two other squares of rational numbers; in other words, for a given rational number {{mvar|k}}, it asks to find rational numbers {{mvar|u}} and {{mvar|v}} such that {{math|1=''k''{{sup|2}} = ''u''{{sup|2}} + ''v''{{sup|2}}}}. Diophantus shows how to solve this sum-of-squares problem for {{math|1=''k'' = 4}}, the solutions being {{math|1=''u'' = 16/5}} and {{math|1=''v'' = 12/5}}.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Thomaidis | first = Yannis
 | doi = 10.1007/s00407-005-0099-8
 | issue = 6
 | journal = [[Archive for History of Exact Sciences]]
 | mr = 2197277
 | pages = 591–640
 | title = A framework for defining the generality of Diophantos' methods in ''Arithmetica''
 | volume = 59
 | year = 2005}}</ref>

Around 1637, Fermat wrote his Last Theorem in [[Latin]] in the margin of his copy of the {{lang|la|Arithmetica}} next to [[Diophantus II.VIII|Diophantus's sum-of-squares problem]]:{{sfn|Dickson|1919|p=731|ps=}}{{sfn|Singh|2022|pp=60–62}}{{sfn|Aczel|1996|p=9|ps=}}

{{Verse translation|lang=la|Cubum autem in duos cubos, aut quadratoquadratum in duos quadratoquadratos & generaliter nullam in infinitum ultra quadratum potestatem in duas eiusdem nominis fas est dividere cuius rei demonstrationem mirabilem sane detexi. Hanc marginis exiguitas non caperet.<ref>[[s:fr:Œuvres de Fermat - I - Partie 2#II|Œuvres de Fermat - I - Partie 2]]</ref>|It is impossible to separate a cube into two cubes, or a fourth power into two fourth powers, or in general, any power higher than the second, into two like powers. I have discovered a truly marvelous proof of this, which this margin is too narrow to contain.<ref>{{cite book|first=T.|last=Heath|author-link=Thomas Heath (classicist)|title=Diophantus of Alexandria|edition=2nd|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1910|pages=144–145}}</ref>{{sfn|Manin|Panchishkin|2007|loc=[https://books.google.com/books?id=wvK586IxaxwC&dq=%22Cubum+autem+in+duos+cubos%2C+aut+quadratoquadratum%22&pg=PA341 p. 341]|ps=}}}}

After Fermat's death in 1665, his son Clément-Samuel Fermat produced a new edition of the book (1670) augmented with his father's comments.{{sfn|Singh|2022|pp=62–66}} Although not actually a theorem at the time (meaning a mathematical statement for which [[mathematical proof|proof]] exists), the marginal note became known over time as ''Fermat's Last Theorem'',{{sfn|Dickson|1919|p=731|ps=}} as it was the last of Fermat's asserted theorems to remain unproved.{{sfn|Singh|2022|p=67}}{{sfn|Aczel|1996|p=10|ps=}}

It is not known whether Fermat had actually found a valid proof for all exponents {{mvar|n}}, but it appears unlikely. Only one related proof by him has survived, namely for the case {{math|1=''n'' = 4}}, as described in the section {{slink||Proofs for specific exponents}}.

While Fermat posed the cases of {{math|1=''n'' = 4}} and of {{math|1=''n'' = 3}} as challenges to his mathematical correspondents, such as [[Marin Mersenne]], [[Blaise Pascal]], and [[John Wallis]],{{sfn|Ribenboim|2000|pp=13, 24}} he never posed the general case.<ref name="van der Poorten-p.5">{{harvnb|van der Poorten|1996}}, Notes and Remarks 1.2, p. 5</ref> Moreover, in the last thirty years of his life, Fermat never again wrote of his "truly marvelous proof" of the general case, and never published it. Van der Poorten<ref name="van der Poorten-p.5"/> suggests that while the absence of a proof is insignificant, the lack of challenges means Fermat realised he did not have a proof; he quotes [[André Weil|Weil]]<ref>{{cite book | first = André|last= Weil|author-link= André Weil | year = 1984 | title = Number Theory: An approach through history. From Hammurapi to Legendre | publisher = Birkhäuser | location = Basel, Switzerland | page = 104}}</ref> as saying Fermat must have briefly deluded himself with an irretrievable idea. The techniques Fermat might have used in such a "marvelous proof" are unknown.

Wiles and Taylor's proof relies on 20th-century techniques.{{sfn|Kleiner|2000|p=33}} Fermat's proof would have had to be elementary by comparison, given the mathematical knowledge of his time.<ref name=macys/>

While [[Harvey Friedman (mathematician)|Harvey Friedman]]'s [[grand conjecture]] implies that any provable theorem (including Fermat's last theorem) can be proved using only [[elementary function arithmetic]],<ref>{{cite book
 | last = McLarty | first = Colin | author-link = Colin McLarty
 | contribution = Fermat's Last Theorem
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-030-19071-2_44-1
 | isbn = 9783030190712
 | pages = 1–23
 | publisher = Springer International Publishing
 | title = Handbook of the History and Philosophy of Mathematical Practice
 | year = 2021}} See p. 21.</ref> such a proof need be 'elementary' only in a technical sense and could involve millions of steps, and thus be far too long to have been Fermat's proof.

=== Proofs for specific exponents ===
{{Main|Proof of Fermat's Last Theorem for specific exponents}}
[[File:Diophantus-VI-24-20-Fermat.png|thumb|right|Fermat's [[infinite descent]] for Fermat's Last Theorem case n=4 in the 1670 edition of the ''Arithmetica'' of [[Diophantus]] (pp. 338–339).]]

==== Exponent 4 ====
Only one relevant [[Fermat's right triangle theorem|proof by Fermat]] has survived, in which he uses the technique of [[infinite descent]] to show that the area of a right triangle with integer sides can never equal the square of an integer.{{sfn|Dickson|1919|pp=615–616|ps=}}{{sfn|Aczel|1996|p=44|ps=}} His proof is equivalent to demonstrating that the equation
<math display=block>x^4 - y^4 = z^2</math>
has no primitive solutions in integers (no pairwise [[coprime]] solutions). In turn, this proves Fermat's Last Theorem for the case {{math|1=''n'' = 4}}, since the equation {{math|1=''a''<sup>4</sup> + ''b''<sup>4</sup> = ''c''<sup>4</sup>}} can be written as {{math|1=''c''<sup>4</sup> − ''b''<sup>4</sup> = (''a''<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup>}}.

Alternative proofs of the case {{math|1=''n'' = 4}} were developed later by many authors.{{sfn|Ribenboim|2000|pp=15–24}}{{refn|group=note|These include [[Bernard Frénicle de Bessy|Frénicle de Bessy]] (1676),<ref>{{cite book|last=Frénicle de Bessy|first=Bernard|author-link=Bernard Frénicle de Bessy|title=Traité des Triangles Rectangles en Nombres|volume=I|year=1676|location=Paris}} Reprinted in ''Mém. ==== Other exponents ====
After Fermat proved the special case {{math|1=''n'' = 4}}, the general proof for all {{mvar|n}} required only that the theorem be established for all odd prime exponents.{{sfn|Ribenboim|2000|pp=1–2}} In other words, it was necessary to prove only that the equation {{math|1=''a''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''b''<sup>''n''</sup> = ''c''<sup>''n''</sup>}} has no positive integer solutions {{math|(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} when {{mvar|n}} is an odd [[prime number]]. This follows because a solution {{math|(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} for a given {{mvar|n}} is equivalent to a solution for all the factors of {{mvar|n}}. For illustration, let {{mvar|n}} be factored into {{mvar|d}} and {{mvar|e}}, {{math|1=''n'' = ''de''}}. The general equation
<math display=block>a^n + b^n = c^n</math>
implies that {{math|(''a''<sup>''d''</sup>, ''b''<sup>''d''</sup>, ''c''<sup>''d''</sup>)}} is a solution for the exponent {{mvar|e}}
<math display=block>(a^d)^e + (b^d)^e = (c^d)^e.</math>

Thus, to prove that Fermat's equation has no solutions for {{math|''n'' > 2}}, it would suffice to prove that it has no solutions for at least one prime factor of every {{mvar|n}}. Each integer {{math|''n'' > 2}} is divisible by 4 or by an odd prime number (or both). Therefore, Fermat's Last Theorem could be proved for all {{mvar|n}} if it could be proved for {{math|1=''n'' = 4}} and for all odd primes {{mvar|p}}.

In the two centuries following its conjecture (1637–1839), Fermat's Last Theorem was proved for three odd prime exponents {{math|1=''p'' = 3, 5, 7}}. In 1770, [[Leonhard Euler]] gave a proof of {{math|1=''p'' = 3}},<ref>{{cite book|author-link=Leonhard Euler|last=Euler|first=L.|year=1770|title=Vollständige Anleitung zur Algebra|publisher=Roy. Acad. Sci., St. Petersburg}}</ref> but his proof contained a major gap.{{sfn|Ribenboim|2000|pp=24–25}}{{sfn|Mordell|1921|pp=6–8|ps=}}{{sfn|Edwards|1996|pp=39–40|ps=}} However, since Euler himself had proved the lemma necessary to complete the proof in other work, he is generally credited with the first proof.{{sfn|Aczel|1996|p=44|ps=}}{{sfn|Edwards|1996|pp=40,52–54|ps=}}<ref name=macys>{{cite journal |first=J. J.|last=Mačys |title=On Euler's hypothetical proof |journal=[[Mathematical Notes]] |year=2007 |volume=82 |issue=3–4 |pages=352–356 |doi=10.1134/S0001434607090088 |mr=2364600|s2cid=121798358 }}</ref> Independent proofs were published{{sfn|Ribenboim|2000|pp=33, 37–41}} by Kausler (1802),<ref name="Kausler_1802" >{{cite journal | last = Kausler |first = C. F. | year = 1802 | title = Nova demonstratio theorematis nec summam, nec differentiam duorum cuborum cubum esse posse | journal =Novi Acta Academiae Scientiarum Imperialis Petropolitanae | volume = 13 | pages = 245–253}}</ref> Legendre (1823, 1830),<ref name="Legendre_1830" >{{cite book | last = Legendre |first = A. G. | year = 1915 | title = Quelques formes quadratiques et quelques équations indéterminées | journal = [[Nieuw Archief voor Wiskunde]] | volume = 11 | pages = 45–75| authorlink=Johannes van der Corput }}</ref> [[Axel Thue]] (1917),<ref>{{cite journal|last=Thue|first=Axel|author-link=Axel Thue|year=1917|title=Et bevis for at ligningen <math>A^3+B^3=C^3</math> er unmulig i hele tal fra nul forskjellige tal <math>A</math>, <math>B</math> og <math>C</math>|journal=Archiv for Mathematik og Naturvidenskab|volume=34|issue=15|pages=3–7|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xIFEAQAAMAAJ&pg=RA13-PA1}} Reprinted in ''Selected Mathematical Papers'' (1977), Oslo: Universitetsforlaget, pp. 555–559</ref> and Duarte (1944).<ref>{{cite journal | last = Duarte | first = F. J. | year = 1944 | title = Sobre la ecuación <math>x^3+y^3+z^3=0</math> | journal = Boletín de la Academia de Ciencias Físicas, Matemáticas y Naturales (Caracas) | volume = 8 | pages = 971–979}}</ref>

The case {{math|1=''p'' = 5}} was proved independently by Legendre and [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet]] around 1825.{{sfn|Ribenboim|2000|p=49}}{{sfn|Mordell|1921|pp=8–9|ps=}}{{sfn|Aczel|1996|p=44|ps=}}{{sfn|Singh|2022|p=106}} Alternative proofs were developed{{sfn|Ribenboim|2000|pp=55–57}} by [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] (1875, posthumous),<ref>{{cite book | last = Gauss | first = C. F. | year = 1875 | chapter = Neue Theorie der Zerlegung der Cuben | title = Zur Theorie der complexen Zahlen, Werke, vol. II | edition = 2nd | publisher = Königl. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen | pages = 387–391| authorlink=Carl Friedrich Gauss }} (Published posthumously)</ref> Lebesgue (1843),<ref>{{cite journal | last = Lebesgue | first = V. A. | year = 1843 | title = Théorèmes nouveaux sur l'équation indéterminée <math>x^5+y^5=az^5</math> | journal = [[Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées]] | volume = 8 | pages = 49–70| authorlink=Victor Lebesgue }}</ref> Lamé (1847),<ref>{{cite journal | last = Lamé |first = G. | year = 1847 | title = Mémoire sur la résolution en nombres complexes de l'équation <math>A^5+B^5+C^5=0</math> | journal = [[Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées]] | volume = 12 | pages = 137–171| authorlink=Gabriel Lamé }}</ref> Gambioli (1901),<ref name="Gambioli_1901"/><ref>{{cite journal | last = Gambioli | first = D. | date = 1903{{ndash}}1904 | title = Intorno all'ultimo teorema di Fermat | journal = Il Pitagora | volume = 10 | pages = 11–13, 41–42}}</ref> Werebrusow (1905),<ref>{{cite journal | last = Werebrusow | first = A. Math. Samml.'' for ''Moskovskoe Matematicheskoe Sobranie''.</ref> Rychlík (1910),<ref>{{cite journal | last = Rychlík|first = K. | year = 1910 | title = On Fermat's last theorem for <math>n=5</math>|language=Czech | journal = Časopis pro pěstování mathematiky a fysiky | volume = 39 | pages = 185–195, 305–317| authorlink=Karel Rychlík |doi = 10.21136/CPMF.1910.121877 | doi-access = free }}</ref> van der Corput (1915),<ref name="van_der_Corput_1915"/> and [[Guy Terjanian]] (1987).<ref>{{cite journal | last = Terjanian|first= G. | year = 1987 | title = Sur une question de V. A. Lebesgue | journal = Annales de l'Institut Fourier | volume = 37 | issue = 3 | pages = 19–37 | doi=10.5802/aif.1096| authorlink=Guy Terjanian | doi-access = free }}</ref>

The case {{math|1=''p'' = 7}} was proved{{sfn|Ribenboim|2000|pp=57–63}}{{sfn|Mordell|1921|p=8|ps=}}{{sfn|Aczel|1996|p=44|ps=}}{{sfn|Singh|2022|p=106}} by Lamé in 1839.<ref name="Lame_1839" >{{cite journal | last = Lamé |first = G. | year = 1839 | title = Mémoire sur le dernier théorème de Fermat | journal = [[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences|Comptes rendus hebdomadaires des séances de l'Académie des Sciences]] | volume = 9 | pages = 45–46| authorlink=Gabriel Lamé }}<br/>{{cite journal | last = Lamé | first = G. | year = 1840 | title = Mémoire d'analyse indéterminée démontrant que l'équation ''x''<sup>7</sup> + ''y''<sup>7</sup> = ''z''<sup>7</sup> est impossible en nombres entiers | journal = [[Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées]] | volume = 5 | pages = 195–211| authorlink=Gabriel Lamé }}</ref> His rather complicated proof was simplified in 1840 by Lebesgue,<ref>{{cite journal | last = Lebesgue | first = V. A. | year = 1840 | title = Démonstration de l'impossibilité de résoudre l'équation ''x''<sup>7</sup> + ''y''<sup>7</sup> + ''z''<sup>7</sup> = 0 en nombres entiers | journal = [[Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées]] | volume = 5 | pages = 276–279, 348–349| authorlink=Victor Lebesgue }}</ref> and still simpler proofs were published by [[Angelo Genocchi]] in 1864, 1874 and 1876.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Genocchi | first = A. | year = 1864 | title = Intorno all'equazioni ''x''<sup>7</sup> + ''y''<sup>7</sup> + ''z''<sup>7</sup> = 0 | journal = [[Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata]] | volume = 6 | pages = 287–288 | doi=10.1007/bf03198884| s2cid = 124916552 | authorlink=Angelo Genocchi | url = https://zenodo.org/record/1428472 }}<br/>{{cite journal | last = l'Académie des Sciences]] | volume = 82 | pages = 910–913| authorlink=Angelo Genocchi }}</ref> Alternative proofs were developed by Théophile Pépin (1876)<ref>{{cite journal | last = Pepin | first = T. | year = 1876 | title = Impossibilité de l'équation ''x''<sup>7</sup> + ''y''<sup>7</sup> + ''z''<sup>7</sup> = 0 | journal = [[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences|Comptes rendus hebdomadaires des séances de l'Académie des Sciences]] | volume = 82 | pages = 676–679, 743–747| authorlink=Théophile Pépin }}</ref> and Edmond Maillet (1897).<ref>{{cite journal | last = Maillet |
